transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-31
Time: 15:00 - 15:50 UTC
Duration: ~50 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Priya Patel (NexaHealth VP Eng), Liam O'Connor (Infra), Sara Kim (Data Science)

Summary:
Quick review of pilot metrics from last week's burst window, discuss autoscaling & burst planning for Dedicated pool, confirm next steps for canary/benchmark tests and updated sizing spreadsheet. Follow-ups on config, pre-warm and node types.

Topics: Dedicated sizing, autoscaling policies, burst capacity, pre-warm strategy, queueing/backpressure, cost estimate for 95/99 p95 traffic, testing plan (1hr burst), docs/links shared.

Transcript:
00:00 Avery: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, we wanted to, uh, go over the results from last week's peak window and then walk through the autoscaler config we prototyped. Diego's got the notes.
00:18 Diego: yeah, hi, hi. so quick TLDR: staging run looked good, we hit sustained throughput of about 42k tokens per minute across the two model variants, but we saw latency spikes around the 95th that matched queue depth increases. some of that is down to concurrency settings on the dedicated pool and the burst behavior.
00:37 Priya: can you repeat the tokens per minute, sorry that number came through garbled.
00:42 Diego: yeah, so roughly 42,000 tokens per minute total which maps to about, uh, 700 tokens per second peak across the pool when both instances were hot. so p95 latencies were around 260ms for chat generation during the peak. p50 was fine, about 80ms.
01:05 Liam: that p95 is a bit higher than we'd hoped, our SLA target is 120ms 95th. is that achievable on Dedicated with different config?
01:12 Avery: short answer: yes, we can get closer but it depends on a few knobs — model quantization, node type (A100 vs H100 or cheaper T4s), instance count, and autoscaler policy. we recommended two approaches: conservative reserved nodes for baseline plus burst pool, or more aggressive autoscale with pre-warm.
01:35 Priya: can you define pre-warm here? like what triggers pre-warm and how long it takes to spin up?
01:40 Diego: pre-warm in our setup means keeping a small number of nodes warmed with KV cache active for the model. spin-up time for a node from cold is ~4–6 minutes depending on image + model size, but warm nodes with KV cached state are effectively instant for short bursts. there is also a fast path for model variants that are quantized which cut warm times a bit.
01:58 Sara: any mis-words on KV cache? sometimes in our notes ppl wrote K V cache (chuckles).
02:02 Diego: yeah, transcription aside, the KV cache is key — prefix caching for commonly requested prompts reduced tokens generated by about 12% in those runs.
02:15 Priya: ok, so for our traffic shape — we have 3 big spikes a day, each ~20 minutes, and then a baseline of low chat traffic. we need to plan around those spikes.
02:24 Avery: that's helpful. our suggested pattern: reserve capacity to cover baseline plus small buffer (say 20% headroom), then autoscale nodes to hit peak. important: autoscaler policy should use request queue length + CPU/GPU util signals to avoid over- or under-reacting.
02:40 Liam: what's the recommended cooldown and scale step? we don't want flapping during short spikes.
02:45 Diego: for your profile — short 20-min spikes — we recommend a two-tier policy: fast response tier using pre-warmed nodes (keeps 2–4 nodes ready) and then a slower reactive tier with cooldown ~5 minutes and step size of 1 node. that avoids giant step-ups but still recovers. also we have burst nodes that are cheaper instances that can be spun for short windows; those are billed as burst capacity.
03:10 Priya: how does cost look for that approach vs just reserving a bigger baseline?
03:14 Avery: we ran a quick calc in the spreadsheet — cheapest baseline that hits 99th is pricey because you'd be paying for idle hours. autoscale+burst reduces cost by roughly 25–35% for your traffic shape, but there's a small hit on p95 latency during very sharp spikes unless you pre-warm. we'll attach the numbers.
03:33 Sara: can you share the spreadsheet link?
03:35 Avery: yes — link to sizing/benchmark sheet: https://redwood.example.com/sheets/nexahealth-poc-sizing (note: placeholder link), and I'll send a PDF of the cost rows after this call.
03:48 Liam: on the technical side, is there a graceful degradation policy? we can't have 500s at the peak.
03:54 Diego: yep — we support auto-fallback to a smaller model variant or to a lower-cost quantized path if latency climbs. you can set route policies that prefer latency or cost; during overload we can route to the compat model which increases latency a little but reduces 500s.
04:12 Priya: is that routing per-request or per-session?
04:16 Diego: per-request with sticky options for sessions; you can pin sessions to a model variant for coherence.
04:22 Priya: good. next — the canary: we want to do a peak-hour canary with real traffic shape. what's the plan?
04:28 Avery: plan is: Redwood will update the autoscaler yaml and provide an example. NexaHealth will run a 1hr burst test on staging that mimics the three daily spikes + baseline. upload CSV of request timestamps and latencies to the benchmark sheet. then we'll iterate on cooldowns and pre-warm counts.
04:46 Liam: questions about logs and audit — we need trace-level logs and audit for Private deployment later. do the Dedicated nodes forward audit logs to our SIEM?
04:55 Diego: yes, we can forward logs to your syslog/S3 or integrate with your SIEM. for Private we bind the control plane, but for Dedicated we provide per-request tracing and token-level cost breakdown in the console; we can hook up your SIEM via agent.
05:14 Priya: and encryption/KMS? keys in our KMS?
05:17 Avery: yes we support customer-managed keys and HSM integration for Private; for Dedicated we typically support bring-your-own-KMS for secret material. we'll include the security doc link.
05:28 Sara: there were some odd spikes in the Nakai run last Wednesday — I saw a CPU burst then all requests queued. any theory?
05:34 Diego: likely a GC or an autoscaler step that didn't finish fast enough; also the model variant warm state might have been evicted. we'll correlate node metrics with request traces in the sheet. please attach the exact time, Sara.
05:48 Sara: I will.
05:50 Priya: any blockers from Redwood side for the canary?
05:54 Avery: nothing blocking, we'll share config and help run the canary. Diego will be on-call for config and to triage.
06:00 Liam: for burst nodes — can you clarify instance types? we prefer H100 for consistent low p95 but might try mix with cheaper GPUs.
06:07 Diego: recommended: H100 for low-latency critical paths, A100 is close depending on kernel perf, and cheaper cards for burst. we can test quantized LLMs which run well on cheaper cards. we'll surface cost/latency tradeoffs in the sheet.
06:23 Priya: how do we measure success for the POC? SLA, cost, and fidelity, right?
06:27 Avery: correct — success criteria: p95 latency <=120ms for primary flows (or acceptable routing to compat model), throughput meeting peak without >0.5% 5xx, and cost per 1M tokens under the target we discussed. we'll write that in the next steps.
06:44 Sara: small nit — transcription sometimes mislabels folks as Speaker 1 etc, don't worry.
06:48 Avery: noted. ok let's go into the autoscaler YAML details — Diego?
06:52 Diego: I'll share the example, quick highlights: policy uses two metrics: request_queue_length (primary) and gpu_util (secondary). thresholds: queue_length > 10 triggers scale-up, queue_length < 3 for scale-down with a cooldown of 300s. step size 1 node, max burst nodes = 6 above reserved. pre-warm count 2.
07:16 Liam: can we have scheduled pre-warm for known daily peaks?
07:20 Diego: yes — schedule-based scaling is supported; you can pre-warm nodes on a cron for the peak windows. combined with reactive scaling it's robust.
07:28 Priya: any recommendations on concurrency per model container? we've seen contention with high concurrency and KV cache misses.
07:33 Diego: lower concurrency (2-4) per GPU container preserves KV cache efficiency for chat workloads. higher concurrency increases throughput but can evict cache and spike p95. tune based on seq length distribution.
07:50 Priya: we'll provide seq length histograms.
07:52 Sara: I'll attach that to the sheet.
07:54 Avery: great. recap quickly?
07:58 Priya: yes please.
08:00 Avery: recap: Redwood to share autoscaler yaml + example, updated sizing spreadsheet with cost rows, security doc link. NexaHealth to run 1hr burst staging test, attach logs/CSV, provide seq length histogram. follow-up canary scheduled week of 2026-04-06. action items in CRM.
08:22 Priya: sounds good. thanks everyone.
08:25 Avery: thanks, we'll send notes and links. Diego I'll loop you in on the sheet. bye.

End transcript.
